strengths: The core pessimistic-verification idea is simple to implement and is evaluated broadly across nine models (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3 family) and three datasets, giving reasonably wide empirical coverage.

Efficiency analysis (equivalent output tokens vs. Balanced F1) convincingly shows that simple/progressive pessimistic verification can match or beat long-CoT scaling at lower token cost, which is a practically useful finding for test-time-scaling budgets.

The contrast between majority voting (near-flat performance) and pessimistic verification (steadily improving with more samples) is a clear and interesting empirical observation that is well illustrated (Fig. 3).
The new QiuZhen-Bench dataset, sourced from graduate-level Chinese contests/qualifying exams, fills a gap for very hard, less-contaminated math verification data and is a useful community resource.
The qualitative case studies (Appendix A.3) are detailed and transparent, showing full model transcripts and reasoning, which aids interpretability and reproducibility of the annotation-error claims.
weaknesses: The central claim that 'most FN cases are dataset annotation errors' rests on manual review of only 20, 13, and 15 cases (Table 1) from a single dataset (IMO-GradingBench) and a single problem type (geometry proof cited); this is far too small a sample to support the strong, generalized claim repeated in the abstract that 'performance is in fact underestimated' across models and benchmarks.

QiuZhen-Bench's ground-truth labels are generated by GPT-5 using the very progressive pessimistic method being evaluated (progressive@3/6), creating circularity: the benchmark used to validate the method is labeled by the method itself, which undermines the independence of the evaluation on that dataset.

The core idea (deeming a proof wrong if any parallel/sequential check flags an error) is explicitly stated to be an extension of prior work (Liu et al. 2025, 'previously existing but underexplored'); the main novelty is the specific vertical/progressive decomposition schemes, which is a comparatively modest algorithmic contribution.

Pessimistic verification inherently trades TPR for TNR (Fig. 6 shows notable TPR degradation, especially for weaker models), but the paper leans heavily on Balanced F1 as the primary metric, which can obscure this asymmetry; no analysis is given of downstream costs of increased false-positive-on-correct-proof rates in real applications (e.g., RL training with false negative reward signals).

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds/runs is reported for any of the reported F1/TNR/TPR numbers, despite temperature=1.0 sampling and stochastic multi-query aggregation.

The paper does not compare against other recent verification/agentic grading methods cited in its own related work (e.g., RefGrader, generative verifier scaling of Mahdavi et al. 2025b), so it is unclear how pessimistic verification stacks up against alternative scalable verification approaches beyond simple majority voting and long CoT.

Broad claims in the conclusion about applicability to RL training pipelines, software engineering, and building open-ended prover benchmarks are speculative and not empirically tested anywhere in the paper.

QiuZhen-Bench's PDF-to-problem extraction pipeline (via GPT-5) is validated only by unspecified 'manual spot checks' rather than a systematic audit across the 1,054 extracted problems, leaving extraction quality largely unverified.

strengths: The core idea is simple, practical, and easy to implement without requiring model retraining, and the paper demonstrates it across a wide range of models (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3 family) and three benchmarks, showing broad applicability.

The efficiency framing (equivalent output tokens vs. balanced F1) is a useful practical lens, and the comparison against majority voting and long-CoT scaling is informative for practitioners deciding how to spend inference-time compute on verification.

The curated QiuZhen-Bench dataset, sourced from Yau contest and Tsinghua QiuZhen doctoral qualifying exams, fills a gap by testing graduate-level mathematics beyond IMO/Putnam-style competition problems, and could be a useful resource for the community.

The case study surfacing annotation/labeling issues in existing benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench) is a valuable observation that has implications for how the field interprets verifier 'false negative' rates, and the concrete worked examples in the appendix make the argument tangible and inspectable.
weaknesses: The core technique (declare an error if any one of several redundant checks flags it) is conceptually a simple OR-ensemble over verifier calls; the paper's own related-work section acknowledges this idea already existed in prior work (Liu et al., 2025), which limits the claimed originality to 'variants' (simple/vertical/progressive) that are largely engineering variations on chunking and iteration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The explanation for why pessimistic verification improves error detection while majority voting does not is purely informal ('we can roughly understand this phenomenon as follows'), with no formal model, no analysis of the assumed independence/diversity of parallel checks, and no ablation isolating temperature/sampling diversity from the pessimistic aggregation rule itself.

The central claim that TPR degradation for strong models is 'largely an illusion' rests on a very small, non-blinded manual case study (13, 15, and 20 FN cases across just three model/dataset combinations, only on IMO-GradingBench), classified into critical/minor/nonsense by the authors themselves with no inter-annotator agreement or independent expert re-adjudication reported; this is too small and too subjective to support the paper's strong headline claim that 'performance is in fact underestimated.'

There is a circularity concern in QiuZhen-Bench: its labels were generated using the paper's own progressive@3/6 method (i.e., GPT-5 with the proposed technique), so subsequent evaluation of other pessimistic-verification variants on this benchmark risks being self-confirming rather than an independent validation.

No statistical uncertainty (error bars, confidence intervals, variance across seeds) is reported for any F1/TPR/TNR curve or bar chart, despite the stochastic nature of temperature=1.0 sampling and the paper's own claims of consistent improvement across many models/datasets.

The paper does not compare against other recently proposed error-detection-focused verification approaches mentioned in its own related work (e.g., RL-trained generative verifiers such as Dekoninck et al. 2025, or agentic grading workflows such as Mahdavi et al. 2025a/b); the only baselines used are single-pass verification, majority voting, and long-CoT scaling, which likely understate the competitive landscape.

Dataset curation for QiuZhen-Bench (GPT-5 extracting problems from PDFs, validated only by unspecified 'manual spot checks') lacks rigor and reproducible detail (e.g., no inter-rater reliability, no error rate estimate, no description of how many problems/pages were checked).

The presentation leans heavily on dense appendix case studies with long raw model transcripts, while the main text's key quantitative claims (e.g., 'majority voting has almost no effect,' 'near human expert performance') are not always accompanied by rigorous, statistically grounded support in the main body.

strengths: The core idea (deem a proof incorrect if any of several independent verification passes reports an error) is simple, practical, and clearly motivated by the observation that error-detection recall, not majority consensus, is the binding constraint in proof verification -- and the paper convincingly shows that ordinary majority voting essentially fails at this task while the OR-based pessimistic rule does not (Fig. 3).

Extensive empirical coverage: three benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify, and the newly curated QiuZhen-Bench), nine models ranging from Qwen3-1.7B to GPT-5/Gemini-2.5-Pro/Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and consistent gains in Balanced F1/TNR across essentially all of them (Fig. 6).

The efficiency analysis (equivalent output tokens vs. Balanced F1) is a useful practical contribution, showing that the progressive/simple pessimistic variants can match or beat scaling long CoT under a fixed compute budget, which matters for real deployment.

The manual case study on false negatives is a valuable diagnostic exercise that surfaces genuine annotation problems in existing 'gold' benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench), illustrating a real and underappreciated confound in verifier evaluation.
Reasonable reproducibility support: full prompts for all three workflow variants and for QiuZhen-Bench construction are given in the appendix, and code/dataset links are provided.

The new QiuZhen-Bench dataset, sourced from genuinely hard graduate-level exams (Yau contest, Tsinghua QiuZhen qualifying exams) spanning multiple subfields, is a useful addition that differs in difficulty/domain from existing contest-math verification benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the paper itself states it is 'an in-depth investigation and extension of the previously existing but underexplored idea of pessimistic verification (Liu et al., 2025)'. The core mechanism is essentially a disjunction-of-independent-detectors ensemble, a well-known idea in anomaly/error detection; the contribution is largely in workflow engineering (simple/vertical/progressive variants) and large-scale empirical characterization rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical insight.

The TPR/TNR trade-off inherent to an OR-rule is not rigorously analyzed. Increasing the number of independent checks necessarily raises TNR while lowering TPR (more chances for a false accusation), and the paper does not compare against a natural baseline that offers the same tunable trade-off, e.g., a single strong verifier with an adjustable decision threshold or confidence score, or weighted/soft ensembling. Without this comparison it's unclear how much of the reported 'improvement' in Balanced F1 is a genuine gain versus a different point on an easily achievable precision-recall curve.

The claim that most false negatives in strong models are due to dataset mislabeling is based on a very small, apparently non-blind manual review (13-20 cases per model, seemingly annotated by the authors themselves) with no inter-rater agreement statistics or independent adjudication. This is a fairly self-serving conclusion (used to argue the method's true performance is 'underestimated') that is not adequately substantiated at this scale.

QiuZhen-Bench's ground-truth labels are generated by GPT-5 using the very progressive-pessimistic method being evaluated (GPT-5 with progressive@3/6). This creates a circularity: when the paper subsequently evaluates other models' verification performance against these GPT-5-derived labels, results are implicitly biased toward the paper's own method and toward GPT-5-consistent judgments, especially given the case studies show that even 'critical' error flags from this labeling process can be subjective (minor/rigor-related) rather than unambiguous.

No comparison against other established test-time-scaling or verification-enhancement baselines beyond majority voting and long CoT (e.g., generative verifier scaling methods, weighted ensembles, or debate-style approaches cited in Related Work), which limits the ability to contextualize how much of the gain is specific to the pessimistic OR-rule versus general multi-sample scaling.

No error bars, variance estimates, or statistical significance testing are reported across the many scaling curves and bar charts, despite results being generated with temperature 1.0 (explicitly to induce sampling diversity), making it hard to assess how robust the reported differences are.

Downstream utility (e.g., actually plugging pessimistic verification into an RL training loop, as motivated at length in the Introduction and Conclusion) is not demonstrated; the broader claims about enabling long-horizon tasks and training pipelines remain speculative and unvalidated within the paper.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated problem (inefficiency and unreliability of LLM-based verification for open-ended math) and proposes a simple, intuitive family of methods (simple/vertical/progressive pessimistic verification) that are easy to implement and reason about.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three verification benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify, and the newly constructed QiuZhen-Bench), multiple model families/sizes (GPT-5 series, Gemini series, Qwen3 series, DeepSeek, Claude), and both verification-only and end-to-end problem-solving settings (IMO 2025, MathArena Apex 2025) provides fairly broad support for the core claims.

Efficiency analysis is reasonably thorough: token-based efficiency curves, auxiliary wall-clock/cost measurements (Table 4), and comparisons against majority voting and long-CoT baselines make a credible case that progressive pessimistic verification is more compute-efficient than naive parallel verification or CoT scaling.

The manual case study on false negatives (Table 2, Appendix A.4) is a valuable and rare form of due diligence — it surfaces genuine annotation errors in existing benchmarks and adds nuance/credibility to the claim that stronger models' true capabilities are underestimated by current benchmarks.
The paper is transparent about prompts (full templates provided in the appendix) and provides some construction details for the new QiuZhen-Bench dataset, aiding reproducibility to a degree.

The discussion section offers a reasonably articulated 'error-centric' and 'segment-wise partitioning' philosophy that could generalize beyond math verification (e.g., code review), which is a modest but genuine contribution to intuition-building in the area.
weaknesses: The core mechanism (reject if any of n/k parallel checks flags an error) is a fairly incremental combination of well-known ideas (ensembling with OR-aggregation, hierarchical/step-level decomposition of verification) rather than a conceptually novel algorithm; the main novelty claim rests on the specific progressive/pruning combination, which is a relatively modest technical contribution.

The central quantitative results rely heavily on benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify) that the paper itself argues are unreliable/noisily annotated for strong models. This creates some tension: the paper uses these same 'unreliable' benchmarks for its main efficiency/performance comparisons (Figures 4-5) while separately claiming their unreliability undermines interpretation of TPR degradation. This weakens the strength of the main quantitative claims for the most capable models.

The case study supporting the 'annotation errors' narrative (Table 2) is very small in scale (10-20 FN cases per model) and involves subjective critical/minor/nonsense classification performed by the authors themselves (not independent experts), raising concerns about confirmation bias and limited statistical reliability of this key qualitative claim.

The problem-solving experiments on IMO 2025 (Table 3) are based on a single run over only 6 problems with manual grading, and Apex 2025 results (Figure 7) show noisy, non-monotonic accuracy curves across only 3 trials with a 12-problem dataset; the observed 'clear advantage' of progressive verification is asserted rather than statistically substantiated (no confidence intervals, no significance testing) despite explicitly noting high variance.

Hyperparameter selection (e.g., progressive@3/6) is not well justified in the main text — it is unclear how sensitive results are to this choice, whether it was tuned on any of the reported test sets, and whether it generalizes across models/domains, raising a risk of overfitting the demonstrated results to a favorable configuration.

The efficiency metric ('equivalent output tokens', with different weighting formulas seemingly chosen per-model, e.g., Output+Input/8 vs Output+Input/6) is somewhat ad hoc and not rigorously justified against real-world deployment costs (e.g., latency, parallel API rate limits are not accounted for despite claiming parallel methods are 'faster').

The vertical pessimistic verification variant is introduced and evaluated but plays a fairly marginal role in the final method (progressive), and its added value beyond simple parallel repetition is only loosely established; the ablation isolating the contribution of decomposition vs. simple repetition (e.g., an explicit progressive vs. vertical vs. simple with matched budget across all reported settings) could be more systematically presented.

The QiuZhen-Bench dataset, used to evaluate weaker models, is itself annotated by GPT-5 rather than human experts, and this is justified only by asserting GPT-5's annotation reliability via the same self-referential case study; this circularity (using a model to validate a model's own verification benchmark) is a notable limitation not fully addressed.

The paper does not report inter-verifier disagreement statistics or false-positive analysis in comparable depth to the false-negative case study, leaving an incomplete picture of the pessimistic method's overall error profile (particularly whether pessimism substantially over-rejects correct proofs in practice, beyond aggregate TPR numbers).

Limited discussion of when/why pessimistic verification might fail (e.g., adversarial or subtly flawed proofs that evade all parallel checks, or cases where decomposition breaks necessary cross-step context) constrains the reader's ability to gauge the boundary conditions of the approach.

strengths: The paper proposes an intuitively clear taxonomy of pessimistic verification (simple, vertical, progressive) and the progressive variant's adaptive, pruning-based decomposition is a sensible engineering idea that could plausibly improve the cost/accuracy trade-off of LLM-based proof verification.

The experimental scope is broad: three verification benchmarks (including a newly constructed QiuZhen-Bench spanning graduate-level math), 8-11 different LLMs, and two downstream agentic problem-solving evaluations (IMO 2025, MathArena Apex 2025).

The observation that existing human/expert-annotated verification benchmarks contain systematic ground-truth errors that disproportionately penalize stronger verifiers is a useful and under-appreciated point for the community, and the paper supplies several convincing worked examples in the appendix.
Reasonably detailed documentation of prompts and workflow diagrams supports partial reproducibility.
The reported ~4x token/cost reduction at comparable Balanced F1 for progressive vs. simple pessimistic verification (Table 4, Figure 4) is a practically relevant efficiency claim if it holds up.
weaknesses: The paper's central quantitative evidence (TPR/TNR/Balanced F1 in Figures 4-5, Table 1) is computed against benchmarks that the authors themselves show to be substantially mislabeled for strong models (Section 3.4, Table 2). This creates an internal contradiction: the main scaling and comparison results rely on noisy labels the paper argues cannot be trusted, undermining the soundness of the primary results rather than just being an acknowledged limitation.

The case study used to argue that benchmark labels are unreliable (Table 2) is based on manual, author-conducted review of only 10-20 FN cases per model with subjective 'critical/minor/nonsense' categories; this is too small and too informally validated (no inter-rater agreement, no blinding) to support the strong claim that 'verification capability of stronger models is substantially underestimated,' which is then used to justify discounting unfavorable TPR trends.

The core mechanism (rejecting a proof if any of several independent verification passes flags an error) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors to already be mainstream practice in several cited systems (DeepSeekMath-V2, Seed-Prover, Huang & Yang 2025); the genuinely new element is restricted to the proof-chunking/progressive-pruning procedure, which is a comparatively modest algorithmic contribution dressed in broader conceptual framing ('pessimistic verification,' 'error-centric philosophy').

The problem-solving experiments (Table 3, Figure 7) are extremely small-scale (6 and 12 problems respectively) with manual grading, no inter-annotator statistics, and only partial repetition (3 trials only for Apex, none for IMO). Token budgets across compared methods differ by an order of magnitude (129K vs. 1,310K vs. 985K in Table 3), confounding any clean comparison of verification-method quality versus simple compute scaling. Problem 5 in Table 3 actually gets worse with verification (6 to 4), an anomaly that is not analyzed or explained, suggesting the method can also hurt performance.

Efficiency/scaling claims are demonstrated mainly on two mid-sized models (GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-30B-A3B); the authors explicitly exclude scaling experiments on frontier models 'since these benchmarks are already unreliable for them,' which is precisely the regime where the paper's significance claims (pushing the frontier of SOTA models) most need support but is least rigorously tested.

No statistical uncertainty (confidence intervals, variance across seeds/datasets) is reported for the main benchmark curves in Figures 3-5, despite temperature=1.0 sampling and documented high variance (explicitly noted for Apex 2025). This weakens confidence in the reported performance differences between pes@n, vp@k, and prog@n/k.

QiuZhen-Bench's ground-truth annotations are generated by GPT-5 itself, then used to evaluate GPT-5 and other models' verification ability; this raises circularity and self-preference concerns that are not adequately addressed beyond a brief note that manual spot checks found no errors in problem *extraction* (not in correctness-annotation of solutions).

Hyperparameters (e.g., progressive@3/6) appear to be fixed across highly heterogeneous datasets/models without clear justification or sensitivity analysis beyond the preliminary scaling plots, raising concern about cherry-picking or lack of principled tuning.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate ('none which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), which is insufficient given the paper explicitly discusses implications for automating frontier mathematical research and pushing capability frontiers of SOTA models.
The code repository link is not provided in the submission (placeholder only), limiting independent verification of the pipeline and case-study claims at submission time.

The concluding discussion makes broad, speculative claims (applicability to software engineering debugging, verification as 'core part of general intelligence') that are not empirically supported anywhere in the paper and read as overreach relative to the actual scope of experiments.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-examined problem: cost-efficient, generalizable automatic verification for open-ended (non-rule-checkable) math proofs, which is central to current agentic math-solving and RL pipelines.

The core idea is simple and well-motivated (error-centric, pessimistic aggregation amplifies the low-probability event of catching an error), and the progressive variant's multi-scale decomposition is a sensible, non-trivial extension over naive repeated verification or fixed-granularity chunking.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span multiple verification benchmarks (Hard2Verify, IMO-GradingBench, a newly constructed QiuZhen-Bench) and many models of different sizes/families (GPT-5 family, Gemini 2.5/3 family, DeepSeek, Claude, Qwen3 family), with consistent trends.

Efficiency is treated seriously via an 'equivalent output token' metric and explicit comparisons against long-CoT and naive pessimistic verification, plus auxiliary wall-clock/cost measurements in the appendix, which strengthens the practical relevance of the claimed efficiency gains.

The downstream agentic problem-solving validation on IMO 2025 and MathArena Apex 2025 with a concrete iterative workflow is a nice complement to benchmark-only evaluation and shows the method is not purely a benchmark artifact.

The manual case-study analysis (Table 2, Appendix A.4) that surfaces concrete annotation errors in existing 'gold' benchmarks is a valuable and interesting finding for the community, with enough worked examples to allow readers to judge plausibility for themselves.
The paper is reasonably transparent about trade-offs it observes (e.g., TPR degradation, occasional over-rejection of correct solutions in the Apex experiments) rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The central claim that TPR degradation under stronger models is 'illusory' due to mislabeled benchmarks rests on a small, author-conducted manual review (10-20 FN cases per model) with subjective 'critical/minor/nonsense' categories and no independent annotator or inter-rater agreement reported; this is a load-bearing empirical argument for interpreting the main results, so its evidentiary weight seems overstated given the small, self-assessed sample.

QiuZhen-Bench's ground-truth annotations are themselves generated by GPT-5, creating circularity when GPT-5 or similarly capable models are later evaluated as verifiers or solvers using this benchmark; the validity of using an LLM to both generate problems/solutions and serve as ground-truth arbiter is not independently verified beyond informal 'manual spot checks.'

Methodological novelty is modest: 'reject if any parallel check flags an error' is essentially an OR-aggregation/pessimistic pooling strategy that the paper itself notes is already implicit in several cited pipelines (DeepSeekMath-V2, Seed-Prover, etc.); the paper's contribution is largely the systematic ablation plus the progressive segmentation heuristic, and hyperparameter choices (n, k, progressive@3/6) appear fixed heuristically without a principled selection procedure or sensitivity analysis beyond the scaling curves shown.

Downstream problem-solving evaluations are on very small test sets (6 problems for IMO 2025, 12 for Apex 2025), and although 3 trials were run for Apex, no formal variance/significance reporting is given; Table 3 also shows per-problem cases where verification-based workflows do not help or even underperform direct prompting (e.g., P5), which tempers the strength of the aggregate efficiency/accuracy claims.

No direct, controlled comparison against other established verification/refinement strategies from the literature (e.g., PRMs, LLM-judge ensembles, or other step-level verifiers) under the same compute budget; comparisons are mainly against the paper's own baselines (standard, majority voting, simple pessimistic) rather than external SOTA verification methods.

The discussion section makes several broad, speculative claims (applicability to software engineering/code debugging, verification as 'core part of general intelligence') that are not empirically supported anywhere in the paper and read as overreach relative to the scope of experiments.

Code/link availability is referenced ('Code is available at') but no link is provided in the visible text, leaving reproducibility of the exact pipeline, prompts beyond those shown, and dataset construction scripts only partially verifiable from the manuscript alone.
